vignette:
She grows up in a home where the loudest sounds are never neutral. As a child in a Middle Eastern family, she learns early to read the air in the apartment: the sharp change in her mother's breathing, the way her father's footsteps land harder when he is angry, the sudden silence before the first blow. She does not remember a single beginning to the violence so much as a pattern that repeats until it feels like the shape of her childhood. When the fighting starts, she hides in closets, behind a couch, or in the bathroom with the faucet running, pressing her hands over her ears and trying to make herself smaller. She often stays awake listening for the next crash, the next scream, the sound of her mother crying through the wall. Even then, she already knows what it means to brace herself.

What stays with her most is not only what she sees, but the helplessness of it. She wants to intervene, to run between them, to call for help, but she is a child and understands that her voice has no power in that room. She becomes skilled at anticipating danger, at noticing the first signs that tension is rising. She watches everyone's faces, the set of a jaw, the speed of a movement, and she carries that vigilance into the rest of her life. At school, she is quiet and alert, easily startled by sudden noise, often drifting away in class when her mind slips back home to what might be happening behind a closed door. She learns to function while carrying dread like a second body.

As she gets older, she becomes good at looking composed. She is charming when she needs to be, careful not to draw attention to herself. She leaves home as soon as she can, telling herself that distance will soften the memories. Instead, the memories travel with her. In her twenties, she starts working as a bartender, a job that suits the part of her that knows how to read people quickly and keep a calm face in the middle of tension. She can handle a crowded bar, the overlapping demands, the late nights, the men who test boundaries. She is often the one who notices when a couple's argument begins to sharpen, when someone's tone changes, when a hand lingers too tightly on an arm. She is good at de-escalation because she has spent years living inside escalation.

At the same time, the bar keeps her on edge. Raised voices from the other end of the room make her body go rigid before her mind catches up. A glass breaking can send a jolt through her chest so sudden it feels like being back in childhood, waiting for the next удар of violence she cannot stop. She covers the reaction by moving faster, refilling drinks, wiping down the counter, keeping busy so no one notices her hands shaking. She sleeps poorly, waking from dreams she does not always remember but that leave her exhausted and tense in the morning. She avoids certain streets, certain songs, and especially any situation that feels like a couple fighting in public, because it makes her stomach knot and her thoughts race to images she has tried for years to bury.

Her marriage briefly gives her the hope of a different life. She wants safety, predictability, and a home that does not feel like a battlefield. But she is also wary from the start, scanning for signs of anger, keeping herself emotionally guarded, and bracing for disappointment. Over time, her distrust and need for control strain the relationship. She is easily startled when her husband moves abruptly or raises his voice, and she has trouble explaining why ordinary conflict feels unbearable to her. Eventually they divorce, and although the separation is painful, it also confirms something she has long feared: closeness can turn dangerous without warning.

Now, at 30, she moves through the world as if part of her is always listening for trouble. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants, checks exits without thinking, and feels uneasy when someone stands too close behind her. She has moments when she feels detached from the present, as though she is watching her life from a few feet away. Some nights she goes home from work and can still hear echoes of shouting in the silence of her apartment, her body unwilling to fully settle even when nothing is wrong. She misses periods of calm because calm itself can feel suspicious. What she knows most deeply is that the violence of her childhood did not end when the fighting stopped; it taught her nervous system to keep waiting for the next blow.
